12410: A prairie is a large, open stretch of land that is covered mostly by grasses and wildflowers, with very few trees or sometimes none at all. Think of it as nature's giant green carpet — wide, mostly flat or gently rolling, and stretching as far as the eye can see in every direction. The sky feels enormous above a prairie because nothing tall is blocking your view.
What Makes a Prairie a Prairie?

Three things define a prairie:

Grasses, not trees. The dominant plant life is grass. Not the short grass of a lawn, but wild grasses — some ankle-high, some taller than a human being. Wildflowers grow among the grasses too, dotting the landscape with color. Trees are rare, and where they do appear, it's usually along the banks of a stream or river.

Rich, deep soil. Prairie soil is some of the most fertile on Earth. Over thousands of years, grasses have grown, died, and decomposed, building up thick layers of dark, nutrient-rich soil. This is why much of the world's most productive farmland today sits where prairies once were.

A specific climate. Prairies receive a moderate amount of rainfall — enough to sustain grasses and wildflowers, but not enough to grow dense forests. They also experience wide temperature swings: very hot summers and bitterly cold winters. Wind is a constant companion, sweeping almost unobstructed across the open land.

Prairies are most associated with North America. The Great Plains — a massive region running through the middle of the United States and into Canada — is the world's most famous prairie landscape. States like Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, the Dakotas, and the Canadian provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are classic prairie territory.

However, similar grasslands exist on other continents under different names. In South America, they're called the pampas. In Central Asia and Eastern Europe, they're called the steppe. In Africa, grasslands of a tropical kind are called savannas. But the word "prairie" specifically and most naturally refers to the North American version.

Not all prairies are identical. They differ mainly based on how much rainfall they receive, which directly affects how tall the grasses grow.

Tallgrass prairies receive the most rainfall and are found in the eastern part of the Great Plains, in places like Iowa and Illinois. The grasses here can grow extraordinarily tall — sometimes well above your head, reaching over 2 meters (nearly 7 feet). These prairies once looked like a sea of swaying green waves.

Mixed-grass prairies sit in the middle, geographically and in terms of rainfall. The grasses are medium-height, typically reaching somewhere between your knee and your waist. Kansas and Nebraska are good examples.

Shortgrass prairies are found further west, where the land is drier. Grasses here stay short — only ankle to knee height. Eastern Colorado and Wyoming are typical shortgrass prairie regions.

Prairies are teeming with life, even if the landscape looks simple from a distance.

The most iconic prairie animal is the American bison (commonly called the buffalo). Millions of these massive, shaggy animals once roamed the prairies in enormous herds — herds so large they could take days to pass. Today, bison populations are much smaller, mostly in protected areas.

Prairie dogs are small, burrowing rodents that live in large underground colonies called towns. Despite the name, they are not dogs at all — they got their name from the bark-like sounds they make to warn each other of danger. Their burrows also provide homes for many other animals.

Other prairie wildlife includes pronghorn antelope (the fastest land animal in North America), coyotes, jackrabbits, badgers, rattlesnakes, meadowlarks, hawks, burrowing owls, and countless insects, including bees that are critical for pollinating wildflowers.

Fire is also a natural and important part of prairie life. Prairie fires — started by lightning or, historically, by Indigenous peoples — regularly swept across the land. Rather than destroying the prairie, fire actually maintains it. It kills off any young trees that might try to take root, clears away dead plant material, and releases nutrients back into the soil, allowing grasses to grow back stronger than ever.

For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples of North America — such as the Lakota, Comanche, Cheyenne, and many others — lived on and with the prairie. They hunted bison, used the grasses, and shaped their cultures around the rhythms of this landscape.

When European settlers arrived in the 1800s, they called the prairie the "frontier" — a vast, open, and seemingly endless land. The famous covered wagons (sometimes called "prairie schooners," because they looked like ships sailing across a sea of grass) carried thousands of settlers westward across the prairie.

As settlers arrived, they quickly realized how extraordinarily fertile the prairie soil was. Over the following century, the vast majority of North America's original prairie was plowed under and converted into cropland. Today, it is estimated that less than 4% of the original tallgrass prairie still exists in its natural form, making it one of the most endangered ecosystems on Earth. The prairies that remain are deeply valued by conservationists and ecologists.

If you were standing in the middle of a prairie, here is what you would experience. The land around you would be open and vast, with an enormous sky overhead. The wind would be almost constant, making the grasses ripple and sway in waves. Sounds would carry far — a meadowlark's song, the rustle of grass, the distant call of a hawk. In summer, the air might smell of dry earth and wildflowers. In winter, the same open land could feel bitterly exposed, with cold winds sweeping across with nothing to slow them down.

There's a particular kind of beauty to prairies that takes time to appreciate. They don't have dramatic mountains or dense forests. Their beauty is in their scale, their openness, their subtlety — the way the light changes across the grass, the sky that seems to go on forever, and the sense that you are standing in the middle of something ancient and alive.

You'll often see "prairie" used as a describing word (modifier) in compound terms:

Prairie dog — the burrowing rodent described above.
Prairie chicken — a type of wild bird native to grasslands.
Prairie fire — a wildfire spreading across open grassland.
Prairie wind — the persistent, sweeping wind characteristic of open prairie land.
Prairie schooner — a historical term for the covered wagons used by settlers.
On the prairie — a phrase meaning out in the open grassland, often evoking a sense of remoteness or frontier life.

It helps to understand what a prairie is not, by comparing it to similar-sounding concepts.

A meadow is a small, grassy open area, often surrounded by trees or forest. A meadow fits in a field; a prairie stretches for hundreds of miles. A meadow is local; a prairie is regional or continental in scale.

A plain (or "the plains") is a broader geographic term for any large, flat area of land. All prairies are plains, but not all plains are prairies — a plain could be desert, tundra, or farmland.

A savanna is a tropical grassland with scattered trees, found mainly in Africa and parts of South America. Unlike a prairie, a savanna has many more trees spread throughout it, and it exists in a hot, tropical climate year-round.

A steppe is the Eurasian equivalent of a prairie — a vast, dry, temperate grassland found across Russia, Central Asia, and Eastern Europe. It tends to be slightly drier and less biodiverse than a North American prairie.

A prairie is not just a pretty landscape — it is a complete ecosystem, meaning it is a finely balanced, interconnected web of life. The grasses feed the insects, the insects feed the birds, the grasses shelter the burrowing animals, the burrowing animals aerate the soil, the fires clear the old growth, and the rich soil feeds the grasses again. Remove one piece, and the rest is affected. This is why the loss of so much of the world's original prairie is considered a significant ecological crisis, and why efforts to restore and protect remaining prairies are so important.

In short: a prairie is one of Earth's great natural landscapes — wide, grassy, windswept, ancient, and far more alive and complex than it first appears.
12411:
When you praise someone or something, you express — out loud or in writing — that you think they are good, worthy, or admirable. You are openly showing approval and admiration.

The key word is express. Praise is not just a feeling inside you. If you only think "that was wonderful" but say nothing, you haven't praised anyone. You must put it out into the world — through words, speech, or writing — for it to count as praise.
Who or what can you praise?

You can praise almost anything:

  • A person — for their work, effort, character, or achievement.
  • A creative work — a novel, a film, a painting, a meal.
  • An action or decision — a policy, a plan, a choice.
  • God or a deity — in a religious sense, to worship and glorify them (this is a very common use of "praise" in religious contexts: "Praise the Lord.")
How to use it in a sentence

The most natural pattern is:

Praise + someone + for + something

  • "The teacher praised her student for the excellent essay."
  • "The manager praised his team for finishing the project on time."
  • "Critics praised the director for her bold vision."

You can also praise something directly, without "for":

  • "The judges praised the performance."
  • "Everyone praised the chef's cooking."

Not all praise is equal. The strength of praise can vary:

  • Mild: "She praised the effort, though the result wasn't perfect."
  • Warm: "The professor praised the student's clear thinking."
  • High/lavish: "Critics lavishly praised the novel as a once-in-a-generation work."

Words like highly, warmly, lavishly, enthusiastically, widely are often used with "praise" to show how strong or intense the praise is.

Praise vs. flattery
This is one of the most important distinctions. Praise is genuine — you say something positive because you truly believe it. Flattery is hollow and insincere — you say nice things not because you mean them, but because you want something in return or want to make someone feel good for a selfish reason. Flattery can feel like praise, but it's empty. Genuine praise, by contrast, is earned and sincere.

Praise vs. compliment
A compliment is usually smaller and more personal — often about appearance or a specific quality ("You have a great smile," "That was a smart question"). Praise is broader and usually about effort, achievement, ability, or character. Praise also often carries a slightly higher level of admiration than a simple compliment.

These words are close to "praise" but have slight differences in tone:

  • Commend — more formal; often used in professional settings. "The committee commended her research."
  • Applaud — can be literal (clapping) or figurative (expressing strong approval). "We applaud this decision."
  • Laud — very formal and elevated in tone; used in writing more than speech. "The critics lauded the performance."
  • Extol — enthusiastic, almost passionate praise. "He extolled the virtues of the new approach."
  • Acclaim — usually public, enthusiastic, widespread praise. "The book was widely acclaimed."

All of these mean roughly the same thing, but they differ in how formal they sound and how intense the praise feels.

If you sing someone's praises, you praise them very enthusiastically — often to other people, not just to the person themselves.

  • "She's always singing her mentor's praises to everyone she meets."
  • "The CEO sang the team's praises at the company meeting."
What is the opposite of praise?
The opposite of praise is criticize — to point out faults or express disapproval. Other opposites include: condemn, censure, blame, disparage, belittle.

• "The coach praised the players after their stunning victory."
  • "Her parents praised her for being honest, even when it was hard."
  • "The film was widely praised by audiences and critics alike."
  • "He praised the volunteers for their tireless dedication."
  • "She gave a speech in which she praised the city's healthcare workers."
To praise is to actively express — through words or writing — that someone or something is good, admirable, or worthy, because you genuinely believe it.
12412:
A pram is a small, four-wheeled vehicle designed to carry a baby. A parent or caregiver pushes it from behind using a handle while walking. The baby lies flat inside it, comfortably and safely, often covered by a hood or canopy to protect from sun, wind, or rain.

Think of it as a cozy, wheeled bed for a baby that can be taken outdoors.

A pram typically has:

  • A deep, basket-like body — large enough for a baby to lie fully flat, like a mini bed on wheels.
  • Four wheels — usually large and sturdy, good for rolling on pavements and paths.
  • A long handle — so the person pushing it can walk upright comfortably behind it.
  • A hood or canopy — which folds up or down to shield the baby from the elements.

The baby inside a pram almost always faces the person who is pushing it, so the parent and baby can see each other. This is an important detail, as you'll see below.
How Is a Pram Different from a Stroller or Buggy?

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

A pram, a stroller, and a buggy all carry babies, but they are not exactly the same thing.

Pram vs. Stroller:
A pram is for very young babies — newborns and infants who cannot yet sit up on their own. Because these babies must lie flat, a pram has a deep, bed-like seat. A stroller (called a pushchair in British English), on the other hand, is for older babies and toddlers who can sit up. Its seat is upright, not flat. The baby in a stroller typically faces away from the pusher, looking forward at the world.

So, in short: pram = baby lies flat, faces the pusher. Stroller = baby sits up, faces forward.

Pram vs. Buggy:
A buggy is generally a lighter, more compact, and foldable version of a pushchair/stroller. It's designed for convenience and travel. A pram, by contrast, is heavier and bulkier but offers more comfort for a very young baby.

"Pram" is primarily British English. You will hear and read this word most commonly in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, and other countries that use British English.

In American English, people rarely say "pram." Instead, Americans say "baby carriage" or "baby buggy" for the same object. If you are reading a British novel, watching a British film, or speaking with someone from the UK, you will almost certainly encounter the word "pram."

The word "pram" has a second, much less common meaning — a type of small, flat-bottomed boat. It has a squared-off front end (called a blunt bow) rather than a pointed one. This kind of pram is used as a small rowing boat or as a dinghy (a small boat used to get to and from a larger boat). You might encounter this meaning in sailing or nautical contexts, but in everyday conversation, "pram" almost always refers to the baby carriage.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

Here are some natural examples to help you "feel" the word in real use:

  • "She parked the pram outside the café while she went in to order coffee."
  • "The newborn slept peacefully in his pram as his mother walked through the park."
  • "Don't leave the baby in the pram unattended."
  • "We need to buy a pram before the baby arrives."

There is also a famous British idiom: "to throw one's toys out of the pram" — meaning to react to a situation in an immature, childish way, like a baby throwing a tantrum. For example: "He threw his toys out of the pram when he didn't get the promotion."

What it isA four-wheeled baby carriage where the baby lies flat
Who uses itParents/caregivers of newborns and young infants
Where the word is usedMainly British English (UK, Australia, NZ, etc.)
American English equivalentBaby carriage / baby buggy
Key difference from strollerPram = flat/lying position; Stroller = upright/sitting position
Secondary meaningA small, flat-bottomed boat (nautical context)

That's everything you need to know about the word pram. It's a simple, practical word, but knowing its regional roots, its distinctions from similar words, and its idiomatic use puts you well ahead of most learners.
12413:
To prance means to move with high, springy, bouncy steps in a way that is lively, energetic, and often showy or self-important. Think of someone — or an animal — who isn't just walking or running, but moving in a way that calls attention to itself: head up, steps light and lifted, full of energy and confidence.

It combines two things at once:

  • A physical quality — light, high, bouncy movement
  • An attitude — confidence, pride, or the desire to be noticed

The most vivid and original use of "prance" is for a horse. When a horse prances, it lifts its front legs high with each step, moves with a proud, controlled energy, and seems almost to be showing off its power and grace. It's not galloping wildly — it's moving in a deliberate, elegant, self-aware way.

This image is the key to understanding the entire word. Whenever you see "prance," picture that horse: lifted steps, energy, and a sense of display.

When a person prances, they move in a way that resembles that horse — bouncy, light on their feet, full of energy, and often with a sense of pride or showiness.

This is where the word becomes interesting, because it can carry different feelings depending on the situation:

1. Playful and carefree (positive or neutral)
Children often prance — they skip and bounce and move with joyful, unself-conscious energy. There's nothing vain about it; they're simply bursting with life.

"The kids pranced around the garden in their costumes."

Here, "prance" just means moving happily and energetically, with that light, bouncy quality.

2. Confident and showy (can be positive or slightly mocking)
When an adult prances, the word often suggests they are very pleased with themselves and want others to notice. This is where "prance" starts to carry a slightly ironic or teasing edge.

"She pranced into the meeting like she had already won the award."

The speaker here is gently mocking her — suggesting she was being a bit too self-satisfied. The movement itself might be perfectly graceful, but the attitude behind it seems a little over the top.

"He pranced around the office after getting the promotion."

Again — the physical movement is energetic and bouncy, but there's an implied eye-roll. He's showing off.

3. A performer or athlete (more neutral to positive)
In performance or sports contexts, prancing can simply describe skilled, light-footed movement done for effect.

"The dancer pranced across the stage."

Here it's largely positive — describing a graceful, energetic performance.

This is crucial for using "prance" correctly. The word almost always carries a slight sense of theatricality — the person or animal is not just moving, they're performing their movement, consciously or unconsciously.

When used about an adult human:

  • It is rarely completely neutral — it almost always suggests some degree of vanity, pride, or self-importance.
  • It is rarely harshly critical either — it's more of a gentle mockery, sometimes even affectionate.
  • The person being described as prancing might not even realise they're doing it.

Think of it this way: if someone walks into a room, they just entered. If someone marches into a room, they're purposeful and serious. But if someone prances into a room, they seem to think the room has been waiting for them.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding "prance" becomes much clearer when you place it next to words that mean similar things:

Strut — To walk with your chest out and shoulders back, in a very deliberate, confident way. Strutting is more horizontal and ground-level. Prancing has more vertical bounce — the steps are higher and lighter. Strutting is cooler and more controlled; prancing is more energetic and springy.

Compare: He strutted down the corridor (slow, deliberate, cool) vs. He pranced down the corridor (bouncy, energetic, showy).

Swagger — To walk with a side-to-side, overly confident motion, usually associated with toughness or arrogance. Much heavier and more aggressive in feel than prancing.

Skip — To move with alternating hops, purely playful, usually for children. No vanity or showiness — just pure joy. Prancing has more self-awareness to it.

Sashay — To walk in a smooth, flowing, hip-swinging way, often associated with glamour or flirtatiousness. Sashaying is more horizontal and fluid; prancing is more vertical and bouncy.

Frolic — To move about playfully and freely, usually without any self-consciousness at all. Prancing has more purpose and display to it; frolicking is more abandoned and carefree.

The key thing that separates prance from all of these: it always has that springy, high-stepping, slightly theatrical quality — like you are very pleased with yourself and your legs know it.

Here are varied examples to help you see the word in action across different contexts:

  1. The white stallion pranced around the edge of the arena, drawing gasps from the crowd.
  2. Little Emma pranced through the living room in her fairy costume, wand held high.
  3. He pranced into the café like a celebrity, though no one there had any idea who he was.
  4. She pranced up to the podium, clearly delighted to have won.
  5. The young deer pranced across the meadow, light and quick.
  6. Stop prancing around and just tell me what happened.
  7. The soldiers pranced their horses down the parade route.
  8. He came prancing out of the dressing room, convinced the suit made him look extraordinary.

Notice how in every example, there is movement that is light, springy, and somewhat self-conscious or showy — whether it's an animal, a child, or a confident adult.

To prance is to move with high, light, bouncy steps in an energetic and often showy way — suggesting pride, confidence, or a desire to be noticed, with a slight but gentle hint of "this person thinks rather well of themselves."
12414:
Prandial means relating to a meal — that is, anything connected to the act of eating, the time of eating, or what happens around a meal. If something is described as "prandial," it is linked in some way to a meal.

That's the whole heart of the word. Everything else below is just that idea applied in different directions.

The word "prandial" on its own is fairly rare in everyday speech. You're unlikely to hear it at the dinner table. It lives primarily in two worlds: medical writing and formal literary writing. But here is the important thing — it becomes extremely common once it teams up with prefixes. Those combinations are everywhere, especially in medicine.

1. Prandial (alone)

Used mostly in clinical or academic writing to mean "relating to a meal" in a general sense.

  • "Prandial insulin" — insulin that a diabetic person takes specifically around mealtimes (as opposed to a background dose taken once a day).
  • "Prandial glucose levels" — a person's blood sugar as it relates to meals.
  • "Prandial conversation" — a formal, slightly old-fashioned way to say conversation that takes place during a meal.

You can see it's a clean, efficient adjective. Instead of saying "insulin taken at mealtimes," a doctor simply writes "prandial insulin."

2. Postprandial — After a meal

This is probably the most common form you'll encounter. Post- means "after," so postprandial means happening or existing after a meal.

  • "Postprandial drowsiness" — the sleepiness many people feel after eating a large meal. (You've almost certainly experienced this even if you've never heard the word for it.)
  • "Postprandial blood sugar" — a person's blood sugar levels measured after they've eaten. Doctors use this constantly when managing diabetes.
  • "A postprandial walk" — a walk taken after dinner. This is a common expression in slightly formal or literary English.

The concept is simple: if it happens after you eat, it can be called postprandial.

3. Preprandial — Before a meal

Pre- means "before," so preprandial means happening or existing before a meal.

  • "A preprandial drink" — a drink taken before sitting down to eat; essentially what most people call an "aperitif." This is the most classic use of the word in non-medical writing.
  • "Preprandial insulin" — insulin a diabetic takes before eating.
  • "Preprandial nausea" — nausea that occurs before a meal, sometimes as a symptom of a medical condition.
The Register and Tone of the Word

"Prandial" is a formal word. It is not informal or colloquial. When a writer or doctor uses it, it signals precision and a clinical or educated tone. In literature, it can carry a slightly elegant, even old-fashioned charm — imagine a Victorian gentleman referring to "prandial pleasures" meaning the enjoyment of a fine dinner.

In medicine, it is used because it is precise and compact. Rather than writing "the patient's blood sugar levels two hours after eating," a clinician writes "postprandial glucose at two hours." Same meaning, far fewer words.

It's worth being precise about what the word doesn't cover:

  • It does not refer to a specific meal (breakfast, lunch, dinner). It is neutral about which meal.
  • It does not describe the food itself. You wouldn't say "prandial soup." It describes the relationship to the meal — the timing, the context, the physiological state.
  • It does not mean "hungry." Hunger is the absence of a meal; prandial is about the meal itself or its surrounding context.
A Quick Mental Picture to Lock It In

Think of a meal as an event with a clear start and end. Everything that happens during that event is prandial. Everything that happens in the lead-up to it is preprandial. Everything that happens in the aftermath is postprandial.

The word is simply a precise label for "meal-related," and it becomes a powerful tool the moment you see it attached to a prefix.

Prandial is a formal adjective meaning relating to a meal, most commonly seen in medical contexts (especially in the combinations postprandial — after a meal — and preprandial — before a meal), and occasionally in literary writing to describe anything connected to the act or occasion of eating.
12415:
A prank is a planned trick that one person plays on another — a deliberate act of deception designed to surprise, startle, fool, or embarrass someone, usually for the purpose of humor. The person doing the trick (the pranker) finds it funny. Ideally, the person being tricked (the victim) eventually finds it funny too.

The important thing to understand is that a prank is not just any joke. It is a physical or situational joke — one that involves doing something to fool someone, not merely saying something.
The key features of a prank

Deception is at the heart of it. A prank always involves tricking someone — making them believe something that isn't true, or placing them in a situation they didn't expect.

It is intentional and planned. A prank doesn't happen by accident. The pranker thinks it through in advance and then executes it. Even something as simple as hiding behind a door to scare a friend is planned — you deliberately chose to hide there and wait.

The victim doesn't know it's coming. That's precisely what makes it a prank. If the other person knew in advance, there would be no trick and no reaction.

The purpose is amusement, not harm. The pranker's goal is to get a reaction — laughter, surprise, confusion, or brief embarrassment — not to genuinely hurt or damage the other person. This is what separates a prank from simple cruelty.

It usually ends with a reveal. After the victim reacts, the pranker typically reveals that it was all a setup: "Gotcha!" or "April Fools!" or "It was just a prank!" This reveal signals that the whole thing was playful, not serious.

• Putting a realistic-looking fake spider in your friend's bag, so they scream when they open it.
  • Telling your sister that school is cancelled tomorrow, watching her get excited, then saying "April Fools!"
  • Wrapping all of your colleague's desk items in gift wrapping paper while they were away.
  • Putting salt in someone's sugar bowl.
  • Hiding behind a door and jumping out to scare a friend.
  • Moving all the apps on someone's phone to different, confusing positions.

In every case, notice the pattern: there is a secret setup, a moment of deception, a reaction from the victim, and then (usually) laughter once the trick is revealed.
The emotional arc of a prank

Pranks typically follow a predictable journey:

  1. The setup — The pranker secretly prepares the trick without the victim knowing.
  2. The fall — The victim encounters the trick and is completely fooled — reacting with surprise, fear, confusion, or embarrassment.
  3. The reveal — The pranker steps forward: "Relax, it was all planned!"
  4. The resolution — Ideally, everyone laughs together — including the person who was just tricked.
How a prank differs from similar words

Prank vs. Joke: A joke is something you say — a funny sentence, a riddle, or a humorous story. A prank is something you do — a physical or situational trick. You tell a joke; you play a prank. (Notice: we always say "play a prank" or "pull a prank" — never "tell a prank.")

Prank vs. Trick: The word trick is broader — it covers magic tricks, clever techniques, and deceptive acts. A prank is a specific kind of trick — one that is humorous and played on a person. All pranks are tricks, but not all tricks are pranks.

Prank vs. Practical joke: These two mean almost exactly the same thing and can be used interchangeably. "Practical joke" is a slightly more formal or old-fashioned way of saying "prank."

Prank vs. Hoax: A hoax is a larger-scale deception — often a false story or lie spread to many people, sometimes with serious intent (like a fake news report). A prank is typically smaller, more personal, and always meant in fun. A prank targets one person or a small group; a hoax often targets the general public.

Pranks have a strong social dimension — they work best between people who trust each other and share a comfortable relationship. Pranking a close friend is very different from pranking a stranger. Between friends, a prank carries an unspoken message: "I know you well enough to know you can handle this, and we'll laugh about it together." With a stranger, the same act might feel threatening, offensive, or simply wrong.

This is why pranks are most common between:

  • Close friends
  • Siblings and family members
  • Classmates or coworkers who know each other well

There are also cultural occasions when pranks are widely expected and accepted. The most famous is April Fools' Day (April 1st each year), a day specifically dedicated to pranks and jokes, when even people who normally wouldn't prank each other feel free to join in.
When a prank crosses the line

Not every prank is harmless. A prank crosses the line when:

  • It causes genuine physical harm — someone gets hurt, not just startled.
  • It causes serious emotional damage — deep humiliation, trauma, or lasting shame.
  • It targets someone who is clearly vulnerable or in a fragile state.
  • Only the pranker finds it funny — the victim is left feeling genuinely hurt, angry, or disrespected, not just briefly embarrassed.
  • It is used as a disguise for cruelty — people sometimes say "it was just a prank" to excuse behavior that was actually mean-spirited from the start.

A good prank ends with the victim laughing too — or at least shaking their head and accepting it with good humor. If the pranker is the only one laughing and the victim is upset or distressed, it has stopped being a prank and has become something unkind.
Common phrases and combinations you'll encounter

• "To play a prank on someone" — the standard way to say you did a prank. ("He played a prank on his teacher.")
  • "To pull a prank" — same meaning. ("She pulled a prank on her whole family.")
  • "It was just a prank!" — what the pranker says after the reveal to reassure the victim.
  • "Prank call" — a phone call made to confuse or trick the person on the other end (sometimes also called a "crank call").
  • "Prank show" — a TV show in which real, unsuspecting people are secretly filmed while being tricked. Famous examples include Candid Camera and Punk'd.
  • "Prank gone wrong" — a phrase used when a prank produces unintended, serious consequences instead of laughs.
The true spirit of a prank

The spirit of a real prank is playfulness — it is rooted in affection and shared humor, not in power or cruelty. When a prank is done well, the victim and the pranker end up laughing together. The joke is on the victim for the moment, but the relationship remains intact — and often becomes a shared, funny memory for years.

When the intent shifts from "let's have fun together" to "let me humiliate or hurt this person," it is no longer a prank in any meaningful sense — it has become something else entirely, with a different word and a different moral weight.

This is the full picture of the word prank: a playful, planned trick between people with a comfortable relationship, meant to amuse — and at its best, to make everyone, including the victim, laugh.
12416:
To prate means to talk on and on — at great length — about things that are trivial, foolish, or unimportant, usually without realizing (or caring) that you are being a bore or a nuisance to others.

It is not just "talking a lot." It is talking a lot about nothing worth saying.

Think of someone at a dinner party who just keeps going and going — talking about their opinions, their petty complaints, or some pointless story — while everyone around them is silently wishing they would stop. That person is prating.

Three things are almost always present when someone prates:

  1. Quantity — They talk far more than the situation calls for.
  2. Shallowness — What they say has little real value, depth, or usefulness.
  3. Obliviousness — They are unaware (or unbothered) that others are bored, irritated, or simply not interested.
The Attitude Hidden Inside the Word

"Prate" carries a strong sense of mild contempt from the speaker's point of view — meaning, the person using the word "prate" is judging the talker negatively. When you say someone prates, you are essentially dismissing what they say as empty noise. You are not just describing their behavior; you are quietly insulting it.

There is also often a hint of pompousness attached to the person who prates. They frequently act as though what they are saying is deeply important or wise — but it isn't. They prate with confidence, which makes it all the more annoying to those who have to listen.
How It Feels to Be Around Someone Who Prates

Imagine a coworker who, every single day, corners you to talk endlessly about politics, conspiracy theories, or how great they used to be in school — repeating the same points, adding nothing new, and never picking up on your body language that screams "please stop." That is prating in everyday life.

It makes the listener feel:

  • Bored
  • Trapped
  • Mildly irritated or exasperated

• "He prated on about his investments for an hour, though nobody at the table cared."
  • "She grew tired of listening to him prate about subjects he clearly knew nothing about."
  • "The politician prated endlessly about reform but said absolutely nothing of substance."
  • "Stop prating and say something meaningful for once."
  • "The old man would prate about his glory days every time we visited."

Notice how in each sentence, the word quietly signals to the reader: this person is annoying, self-absorbed, or simply foolish in their talking.

Many words describe talking too much, but they each have a different flavor:

  • Chatter — fast, light, friendly small talk. Not necessarily annoying; often just casual. Children chatter.
  • Babble — talking rapidly and incoherently, like someone who is confused or overly excited. Focuses more on the incoherence.
  • Ramble — going off-topic, losing the thread of a point. Focuses on losing direction.
  • Drone — talking in a dull, flat, monotonous tone that puts people to sleep.
  • Boast / Brag — specifically showing off. Can overlap with prating when someone prates about themselves.
  • Prate — uniquely combines excessive length + triviality + a touch of pomposity + the judgment of the listener. It is the most dismissive of all these words.

If you want to express that someone talks too much AND that what they say is empty AND that you find it rather contemptible — prate is precisely the word.

"Prate" is a formal and somewhat literary word. You are unlikely to hear it in casual everyday conversation. You will encounter it more in:

  • Classic literature (Shakespeare, 19th-century novels)
  • Formal essays or criticism
  • Educated writing where the author wants to sound precisely dismissive

If you use it in everyday speech, you will sound eloquent and slightly old-fashioned — which in the right context can be very effective.
One Final Way to Remember It

Prate = Pointless + Rate (of talking) that never slows down.

Someone who prates is running their mouth at full speed, going nowhere, carrying nothing of value — and they won't stop.
12417:
A pratfall is a fall in which someone lands hard on their buttocks — their rear end, their bottom. That's the simplest, most direct definition.

But the word carries a very specific flavor. It's not just any fall. A pratfall is a fall that looks sudden, clumsy, and ridiculous — the kind that makes people burst out laughing. Picture a clown in a circus slipping on a banana peel and crashing down on his backside. That is the classic pratfall.

The word is used in two closely related ways:

1. The literal, physical meaning

A pratfall is an actual, physical fall onto your rear end — especially one that is comic or embarrassing to witness. This sense is deeply tied to the world of physical comedy and entertainment.

For decades, comedians, clowns, and actors have used the pratfall as a tool to get laughs. Charlie Chaplin was a master of it. The Three Stooges built entire careers on it. A performer carefully choreographs a pratfall — they deliberately make themselves look like they slipped, stumbled, and flopped to the ground — because audiences find it hilarious.

So even in its most literal sense, the word carries a comic, theatrical energy. When you say someone took a pratfall, you are conjuring the image of something sudden, undignified, and funny.

2. The figurative meaning (this is how the word is most commonly used in everyday language)

Over time, "pratfall" grew beyond the physical. It came to mean an embarrassing blunder, a humiliating mistake, or a spectacular public failure — especially one that makes the person look foolish or incompetent.

This is the metaphorical pratfall: you didn't fall on the floor, but you stumbled in a way that everyone noticed, and now you look ridiculous.

A few examples of the figurative sense:

  • A politician gives an important speech and accidentally insults a large group of voters. His career suffers. People call it a major pratfall.
  • A famous company launches a product with great fanfare, but it fails miserably within weeks. Journalists write about the company's very public pratfall.
  • A celebrated chef opens a new restaurant that gets scorched in reviews and closes in a month. It's called his biggest pratfall yet.

Notice what these have in common: a fall from a position of confidence or competence, witnessed by others, resulting in embarrassment. That's the soul of the word.
What Makes "Pratfall" Special — Its Tone and Connotation

The word is not neutral. It carries a particular tone that separates it from simple words like "mistake" or "failure."

Here's what "pratfall" implies:

  • Suddenness. The failure often comes out of nowhere, catching both the person and observers off guard — just like a physical fall.
  • Undignified quality. There is something inherently un-graceful about a pratfall. It's not a quiet, private failure. It's public and awkward.
  • A touch of dark comedy. The word almost always has a slightly humorous undertone, even when describing something genuinely unfortunate. When you call something a "pratfall," you are subtly suggesting that it had the quality of watching someone slip on a banana peel — there is an absurdity to it.
  • The fall is self-inflicted or avoidable. Pratfalls, in both the physical and figurative sense, often feel like something the person could have avoided. They walked right into it.

Because of this tone, "pratfall" is a favorite word in journalism, political commentary, and satire. Writers reach for it when they want to describe a failure that is both serious and faintly ridiculous — when someone in power stumbles and ends up looking like a fool.

• "The senator's pratfall during the debate — accidentally calling his own bill 'useless' — went viral overnight."
  • "The film was supposed to launch a franchise, but it became the studio's most embarrassing pratfall in years."
  • "After a string of pratfalls, the company finally hired a communications team to manage its public image."
  • "Even the greatest comedians know that a well-timed pratfall can save a scene that isn't working." ← (literal, theatrical use)
  • "Her debut was going perfectly until she mispronounced the guest of honour's name — a pratfall she'll never forget."
How It Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat it emphasizes
MistakeA simple error; no emotional color
BlunderA clumsy, careless mistake; more serious
GaffeA social or verbal slip, usually in public
PratfallAn embarrassing, visible failure with comic or undignified energy — the performance of failure

(A pratfall often contains a gaffe or blunder within it, but it's bigger — it has spectacle and embarrassment baked in.)
The Full Picture in One Sentence

A pratfall is a fall onto one's rear end that looks clumsy and comic — and by extension, any embarrassing, undignified public failure that makes the person look foolish, as if they stumbled and landed flat on their face in front of everyone watching.
12418:
To prattle means to talk continuously about things that are trivial, foolish, or unimportant — in a way that goes on and on, without really saying anything meaningful or worthwhile. The talking is usually rapid, effortless, and hard to stop, almost like a leaking tap that you can't turn off.

Think of it this way: if you asked someone a simple question and they gave you a ten-minute response full of pointless details, irrelevant side stories, and shallow observations — they are prattling.
The Attitude Hidden Inside the Word

This is where it gets interesting. When you use the word "prattle," you are not just describing what someone is doing — you are also quietly judging it. The word carries a tone of mild irritation, impatience, or condescension. It signals that the listener considers the talk to be a waste of time, even if the talker themselves is completely unaware of this.

This makes "prattle" different from a neutral word like "talk" or "speak." Saying someone is prattling is like rolling your eyes while describing their speech.

The word works in two slightly different situations, and the feeling it carries changes subtly between them:

1. When used about children — mild and affectionate

Young children naturally talk about small, unimportant things — their toys, a funny bug they saw, what their imaginary friend did. When "prattle" is used this way, it is not harsh. It is almost endearing. The child is not expected to say anything profound, so the triviality is innocent and even charming.

The little girl prattled happily about her dolls while her mother cooked dinner.

Here, "prattle" feels warm. Nobody is annoyed. It is just the natural, bubbly talk of a child.

2. When used about adults — critical and dismissive

When an adult prattles, the tone becomes much more negative. Adults are expected to have worthwhile things to say, so talking on and on about nothing is considered silly, immature, or irritating. The word implies that the speaker is either foolish, self-absorbed, or simply not aware that they are wasting everyone's time.

He prattled on about his neighbour's garden for twenty minutes while we all quietly suffered.

Here, "prattle" is clearly mocking. The speaker finds the talker tedious.
What Separates Prattle from Just "Talking Too Much"

Talking too much is about quantity — saying more than necessary.

Prattling is about quality — saying things that have no real value or substance, and doing so at length. You can give a long, thoughtful speech and not be prattling. But if you talk endlessly about nothing — gossip, minor complaints, pointless observations — that is prattle, even if it lasts only five minutes.

The two key ingredients are:

  • Triviality — the content is shallow, silly, or unimportant
  • Relentlessness — it keeps going without pause or purpose

She prattled on about her new handbag for so long that I completely zoned out.

Stop prattling and get to the point!

The toddler prattled cheerfully as they walked through the park.

I nodded politely while he prattled, though I hadn't listened in several minutes.

Notice the phrase "prattle on" — this is very commonly used and adds emphasis to the continuous, unstoppable nature of the talking. "On" reinforces that it just keeps going.
How It Compares to Similar Words

There are several words in English that live close to "prattle," but each has its own flavour:

Babble — focuses more on the sound being incoherent or unclear, like sounds tumbling out without structure. A baby babbles. Prattle is more intelligible as speech, but meaningless in content.

Ramble — to ramble is to drift from topic to topic without direction, like a wandering path. Prattle is more about the content being trivial, not necessarily about losing the thread.

Chatter — light, fast, informal talk. Chatter is fairly neutral and social (friends chatting is fine). Prattle specifically implies the content is foolish or worthless.

Blather — very close to prattle. Blather leans toward outright nonsense; prattle leans toward triviality and childishness.

Jabber — rapid, excited, and often hard to follow. Jabber focuses on the pace and confusion; prattle focuses on the pointlessness.

If you had to rank them by how dismissive they sound toward the speaker: prattle and blather are among the more condescending; chatter is the most neutral.
The Register of the Word Itself

"Prattle" is a slightly formal or literary word. You are more likely to read it in a novel, a newspaper column, or hear it from someone who enjoys precise language. In casual everyday conversation, most people would simply say "going on and on" or "talking rubbish." So when someone uses "prattle," they are being a touch sophisticated — and usually a touch sarcastic — about whoever is doing the talking.
To prattle is to talk non-stop about trivial, shallow, or foolish things — and the word itself is a quiet signal that the listener finds it tiresome or silly.
12419:
"Prattle on" means to talk continuously about unimportant or trivial things, in a way that is childish, senseless, or annoying to the listener.

When someone "prattles on," they are not having a meaningful conversation. They are simply rambling — going on and on and on — about things that don't really matter, without realizing (or caring) that the other person has lost interest.

Think of it this way: imagine a child talking non-stop about their toy collection for 45 minutes while the adult in the room is quietly going crazy. That child is prattling on.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Understanding each part of this idiom makes it stick in your memory much better.

"Prattle" is the core word. It originally described the babbling sounds that babies make — sounds that are cute but completely meaningless. Over time, the word expanded to describe adults who talk like babies in the sense that they say a lot but communicate very little of value. The sound of the word itself even feels light and fluttery — prattle, prattle, prattle — which mirrors the kind of airy, weightless talk it describes.

"On" is a small but powerful word here. In English, adding "on" after a verb of action suggests that the action keeps going without stopping. For example:

  • "ramble on" = keep rambling
  • "drone on" = keep droning
  • "go on" = keep going

So "prattle on" = to keep prattling, without end.

Together, the phrase captures both the quality of the talk (silly, empty, unimportant) and the quantity of it (endless, non-stop).
The Feeling / Tone of This Idiom

This is a negative expression. It carries a sense of mild annoyance, boredom, or even gentle mockery.

When you say someone is "prattling on," you are suggesting one or more of these things:

  • They are talking too much.
  • What they are saying is not important or interesting.
  • They are unaware that the listener doesn't care.
  • Their talk is coming across as immature or silly.

It is not a violent or harsh insult. It's more of a soft, slightly impatient criticism. You might roll your eyes when you say it. It has a mildly humorous edge to it, like you're gently making fun of someone rather than attacking them.

Seeing the idiom in action across different situations is one of the best ways to fully absorb its meaning.

Situation 1 — A boring colleague:

"He prattled on about his weekend fishing trip for half an hour. Nobody in the office was even listening anymore."

(He kept talking about something unimportant, not noticing people had tuned out.)

Situation 2 — A child talking non-stop:

"My little cousin prattled on about her dolls the entire car ride. I love her, but I was exhausted by the time we arrived."

(Sweet but tiresome — classic prattling.)

Situation 3 — A nervous person talking too much:

"She was so nervous at the job interview that she prattled on for five minutes about her favourite coffee brand when they asked about her hobbies."

(Talking too much, going off-topic, saying things that don't really matter.)

Situation 4 — A pompous or self-important person:

"The politician prattled on for twenty minutes without actually answering the question."

(Talking a lot, saying nothing of real substance.)

Situation 5 — Used about yourself (self-aware and humble):

"Sorry, I'm prattling on — let me get to the point."

(You can use it about yourself to show you're aware you've been rambling. This comes across as self-aware and polite.)
The Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

The structure is straightforward.

Subject + prattle + on + (about something)

The "about" part is optional, but it's very common to add it to tell the listener what the person was talking about.

  • "She prattled on." ✅ (Fine on its own.)
  • "She prattled on about her diet." ✅ (More specific and natural.)
  • "He kept prattling on about how great his new phone is." ✅ (Adding "kept" makes it even more exhausting-sounding, which is often the point.)

To be razor-sharp in your understanding, it helps to know what this idiom does not mean.

  • It does not mean lying or deceiving. (That would be "making things up" or "spinning a yarn.")
  • It does not mean shouting or arguing loudly. (That would be "ranting" or "raving.")
  • It does not mean speaking with deep authority on a complex topic. (That would be "holding forth" or "lecturing.")
  • It does not mean talking about things that matter and are interesting. A passionate expert explaining their field is not "prattling on" — they are being informative.

The key ingredients for "prattling on" are always: meaningless content + too much of it + not stopping.

These expressions are related to "prattle on," but each has a slightly different flavour. Knowing the differences sharpens your feel for the language.

"Ramble on" — To talk or write in a disorganized way, jumping from topic to topic. A rambler loses their thread. A prattler never had a thread to begin with.

"Drone on" — To speak in a flat, monotonous, dull voice. The focus is on the sound being boring, like the hum of an engine. Prattling is more about the content being trivial.

"Go on and on" — A very casual way to say someone won't stop talking. Less poetic and vivid than "prattle on," but means something similar.

"Babble on" — Very close to "prattle on." Babbling is perhaps even more chaotic — almost incoherent. Prattling is slightly more organized than babbling, but both suggest empty, flowing speech.

"Blather on" — Nearly identical to "prattle on" in meaning. Blathering tends to sound slightly more foolish and pompous. Both are great words to know.

The word "prattle" has been in English since the 16th century. It came from Middle Low German and Dutch words meaning "to chatter" or "to babble." Those older words were used to describe the sounds of young children learning to speak — sounds that are endearing but carry no real meaning.

English borrowed this idea and turned it into a gentle insult for adults who talk too much about too little, essentially comparing them to babbling children. By adding "on," the idiom captures the relentless, unstoppable quality of that kind of talk.

If you ever forget what "prattle on" means, remember this image:

🍃 A leaf in the wind — it moves constantly, it makes a soft rustling sound, it goes wherever the breeze takes it, but it's going nowhere important and carrying nothing of weight.

That's what prattling on is. Lots of movement. Lots of noise. No real destination.
"Prattle on" means to talk continuously, at length, about trivial or unimportant things — in a way that is silly, childish, or tiresome to those listening.
